claim: The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) is a large multi-subunit E3 ubiquitin ligase that controls progression through the cell cycle by orchestrating the timely proteolysis of mitotic cyclins and other cell cycle regulatory proteins.
source: The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) is a large multi-subunit E3 ubiquitin ligase that controls progression through the cell cycle by orchestrating the timely proteolysis of mitotic cyclins and other cell cycle regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about APC/C function supported by extensive prior research and cited in the manuscript.

claim: The overall architectures of human and S. cerevisiae APC/C are conserved.
source: Whereas the overall architectures of human and S. cerevisiae APC/C are conserved, as well as the mechanism of CDH1 inhibition by CDK-phosphorylation, specific variations exist, including striking differences in the mechanism of coactivator-mediated stimulation of E2 binding, and the activation of APC/CCDC20 by phosphorylation.
evidence: The manuscript presents structural comparisons between human and S. cerevisiae APC/C complexes showing conserved overall architecture.

claim: The mechanism of CDH1 inhibition by CDK-phosphorylation is conserved between human and S. cerevisiae APC/C.
source: Whereas the overall architectures of human and S. cerevisiae APC/C are conserved, as well as the mechanism of CDH1 inhibition by CDK-phosphorylation, specific variations exist, including striking differences in the mechanism of coactivator-mediated stimulation of E2 binding, and the activation of APC/CCDC20 by phosphorylation.
evidence: The manuscript presents structural and functional data showing conserved CDK phosphorylation sites and mechanisms for CDH1 inhibition.

claim: In S. cerevisiae apo-APC/C, the catalytic module is already positioned to bind E2, in contrast to human APC/C where coactivator induces a conformational change.
source: In contrast to human APC/C in which coactivator induces a conformational change of the catalytic module APC2:APC11 to allow E2 binding, in S. cerevisiae apo-APC/C the catalytic module is already positioned to bind E2.
evidence: The manuscript presents cryo-EM structures showing the position of the catalytic module in different states.

claim: There is no evidence of a phospho-regulatable auto-inhibitory segment of APC1 in S. cerevisiae that sterically blocks the CDC20 C-box binding site of APC8.
source: Furthermore, we find no evidence of a phospho-regulatable auto-inhibitory segment of APC1, that in the unphosphorylated human APC/C, sterically blocks the CDC20C-box binding site of APC8.
evidence: The manuscript reports absence of cryo-EM density for an auto-inhibitory segment in the unphosphorylated apo-APC/C structure.

claim: The 34-residue tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) motif was characterized through analysis of sequences of proteins encoded by the CDC16, CDC23, and CDC27 genes.
source: Analysis of the sequences of proteins encoded by the CDC16, CDC23, and CDC27 genes led to the characterisation of the 34-residue tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) motif that is usually arranged in multiple copies in contiguous arrays (King et al., 1995; Lamb et al., 1994; Sikorski et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a historical fact about TPR motif discovery supported by citations to prior work.

claim: S. cerevisiae APC/C contains four small subunits: APC9, APC12/CDC26, APC13/SWM1, and APC15/MND2.
source: The isolation of endogenous APC/C from S. cerevisiae confirmed the composition of large APC/C subunits that form a MDa-sized complex, and also the discovery of four small subunits (APC9, APC12/CDC26, APC13/SWM1, and APC15/MND2; Hall et al., 2003; Passmore et al., 2003; Zachariae et al., 1998b; Zachariae et al., 1996), that are also conserved with metazoan APC/C.
evidence: This is supported by prior biochemical studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Coactivator and APC10 cooperate to generate a co-receptor for D-box degron recognition.
source: Coactivator and APC10 cooperate to generate a co-receptor for D-box degron recognition (Brown et al., 2015; Buschhorn et al., 2011; Carroll et al., 2005; Carroll and Morgan, 2002; Chang et al., 2014; Chao et al., 2012; da Fonseca et al., 2011; Hartooni et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by multiple prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Coactivator alone binds the KEN box and ABBA motif degrons.
source: whereas coactivator alone binds the KEN box and ABBA motif degrons (Chao et al., 2012; He et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: CDH1 interacts with the APC/C during G1, whereas CDH1 phosphorylation at the onset of S-phase inhibits its binding to the APC/C.
source: CDH1 interacts with the APC/C during G1, whereas CDH1 phosphorylation at the onset of S-phase inhibits its binding to the APC/C, a process that determines the irreversible transition from G1 into S-phase.
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism of cell cycle regulation supported by prior research.

claim: CDK and polo kinases phosphorylate the APC/C to stimulate CDC20 binding on entering mitosis.
source: On entering mitosis, CDK and polo kinases phosphorylate the APC/C to stimulate CDC20 binding to the APC/C (Golan et al., 2002; Kraft et al., 2005; Kramer et al., 2000; Lahav-Baratz et al., 1995; Rudner and Murray, 2000; Shteinberg et al., 1999; Zachariae et al., 1998a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: S. cerevisiae APC/C utilises a third coactivator (Ama1) to regulate the events of meiosis.
source: In contrast to metazoan APC/C, S. cerevisiae APC/C utilises a third coactivator (Ama1) to regulate the events of meiosis (Cooper et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a prior study cited in the manuscript.

claim: S. cerevisiae APC/C functions using two E2s: a priming E2 (Ubc4) that directly ubiquitylates APC/C substrates, and a processive E2 (Ubc1) that extends these ubiquitin moieties.
source: As for human APC/C, S. cerevisiae APC/C functions using two E2s, a priming E2 that directly ubiquitylates APC/C substrates (Ubc4), and a processive E2 (Ubc1) that extends these ubiquitin moieties (Rodrigo-Brenni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a prior study cited in the manuscript.

claim: The processive E2 that pairs with human APC/C (UBE2S) extends ubiquitin chains through K11 linkages.
source: Whereas the processive E2 that pairs with human APC/C (UBE2S) extends ubiquitin chains through K11 linkages (Garnett et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2008; Matsumoto et al., 2010; Wickliffe et al., 2011; Williamson et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by multiple prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Ubc1 of S. cerevisiae synthesises K48-linked ubiquitin chains.
source: Ubc1 of S. cerevisiae synthesises K48-linked chains (Rodrigo-Brenni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a prior study cited in the manuscript.

claim: Ubc4 and Ubc1 both bind the RING domain of APC11 and compete for APC/C binding.
source: Ubc4 and Ubc1 both bind the RING domain of APC11, and therefore compete for APC/C binding (Girard et al., 2015; Rodrigo-Brenni and Morgan, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Ubc1 possesses an accessory UBA domain that enhances its affinity for the APC/C.
source: Ubc1 possesses an accessory UBA that enhances its affinity for the APC/C (Girard et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a prior study cited in the manuscript.

claim: The activities of both S. cerevisiae and human APC/C are inhibited by the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC).
source: The activities of both S. cerevisiae and human APC/C are inhibited by the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC; Burton and Solomon, 2007; Sudakin et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Acm1 is a specific inhibitor of S. cerevisiae APC/C.
source: whereas Acm1 (Martinez et al., 2006) and EMI1 (early mitotic inhibitor 1; Cappell et al., 2018; Reimann et al., 2001a; Reimann et al., 2001b) are specific to S. cerevisiae and metazoan APC/C, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by a prior study cited in the manuscript.

claim: EMI1 (early mitotic inhibitor 1) is a specific inhibitor of metazoan APC/C.
source: whereas Acm1 (Martinez et al., 2006) and EMI1 (early mitotic inhibitor 1; Cappell et al., 2018; Reimann et al., 2001a; Reimann et al., 2001b) are specific to S. cerevisiae and metazoan APC/C, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: A 4.0 Å resolution structure of the S. cerevisiae APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 complex was determined.
source: We completed building a 4.0 Å structure of the S. cerevisiae APC/CCDH1-substrate complex (APC/CCDH1:Hsl1), allowing a comparative study of the S. cerevisiae and human systems.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Human APC/C contains an additional TPR subunit APC7 that is not present in S. cerevisiae APC/C.
source: While human and S. cerevisiae APC/C architectures are in general very similar, there are significant differences, including the additional TPR subunit APC7 in human APC/C, and the structures of the smaller, less well-conserved subunits.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: In human APC/C, coactivators induce a conformational change of APC2:APC11 from a downwards state to an upwards state competent to bind E2.
source: For example, in contrast to human APC/C, the catalytic module APC2:APC11 of S. cerevisiae adopts an active conformation in the absence of coactivator, whereas in human APC/C coactivators induce a conformational change of APC2:APC11 from a downwards state, in which the E2-binding site is blocked, to an upwards state competent to bind E2 (Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: In human APC/C, phosphorylation of an autoinhibitory (AI) segment within APC1 removes a steric blockade to the binding of the CDC20 C-box to APC8.
source: In human APC/C, phosphorylation of an autoinhibitory (AI) segment incorporated within a long loop of the APC1 subunit removes a steric blockade to the binding of the CDC20 C-box to its binding site on APC8 (Fujimitsu et al., 2016; Qiao et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by prior structural and functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: In S. cerevisiae apo-APC/C cryo-EM maps, there is no evidence of an auto-inhibitory segment bound to the coactivator C box-binding site in APC8.
source: In our S. cerevisiae apo-APC/C cryo-EM maps we observe no evidence of an auto-inhibitory segment bound to the coactivator C box-binding site in APC8.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of cryo-EM density maps presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mechanisms of activation of APC/CCDC20 by phosphorylation are likely not conserved from S. cerevisiae to human.
source: Thus it seems likely that mechanisms of activation of APC/CCDC20 by phosphorylation are not conserved from S. cerevisiae to human.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences observed in the manuscript.

claim: S. cerevisiae APC/C was reconstituted using the baculovirus/insect cell system.
source: We reconstituted S. cerevisiae APC/C using the baculovirus/insect cell system (Zhang et al., 2016c; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), similar to methods described previously (Schreiber et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: When in complex with the CDH1 coactivator, the reconstituted APC/C ubiquitylated the high-affinity S. cerevisiae substrate Hsl1.
source: When in complex with the CDH1 coactivator, the reconstituted APC/C ubiquitylated the high-affinity S. cerevisiae substrate Hsl1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ubiquitylation assay data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Phosphorylated APC/C was generated using CDK2-cyclin A.
source: Phosphorylated APC/C was generated using CDK2-cyclin A, and mass spectrometry revealed the majority of phosphosites mapped to the APC1, APC3 and APC6 subunits (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Mass spectrometry revealed the majority of phosphosites mapped to the APC1, APC3 and APC6 subunits.
source: Phosphorylated APC/C was generated using CDK2-cyclin A, and mass spectrometry revealed the majority of phosphosites mapped to the APC1, APC3 and APC6 subunits (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: A cryo-EM reconstruction of the ternary APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 complex was determined at 4 Å resolution.
source: A cryo-EM reconstruction of the ternary APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 complex was determined at 4 Å resolution (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3 and Table 1)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data and figures.

claim: The structures of unphosphorylated and phosphorylated apo-APC/C were determined at 4.9 Å and 4.5 Å resolution, respectively.
source: whereas the structures of unphosphorylated and phosphorylated apo-APC/C were determined at 4.9 Å and 4.5 Å resolution, respectively (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2, Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2, and Table 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data and figures.

claim: The overall structure of the recombinant APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 ternary complex is similar to the 10 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 determined using native APC/C purified from endogenous sources.
source: The overall structure of the recombinant APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 ternary complex is similar to the 10 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 determined using native APC/C purified from endogenous sources (da Fonseca et al., 2011), and our earlier negative stain EM reconstruction (Schreiber et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: The APC/C complex adopts a triangular structure delineated by a lattice-like shell that generates a central cavity.
source: The complex adopts a triangular structure delineated by a lattice-like shell that generates a central cavity (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 1.

claim: The APC/C is comprised of two major modules: the TPR lobe and the platform module.
source: The APC/C is comprised of two major modules; the TPR lobe composed of the canonical TPR subunits APC3/CDC27, APC6/CDC16 and APC8/CDC23, and the platform module composed of the large APC1 subunit, together with APC4 and APC5.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the structural data.

claim: The TPR lobe adopts a quasi-symmetric structure through the sequential stacking of three structurally related TPR homo-dimers.
source: The TPR lobe adopts a quasi-symmetric structure through the sequential stacking of the three structurally related TPR homo-dimers, APC8/CDC23, APC6/CDC16 and APC3/CDC27.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Each TPR protein is composed of 12–13 copies of the TPR motif.
source: Each TPR protein is composed of 12–13 copies of the TPR motif, a 34-residue repeat that forms a pair of anti-parallel α-helices.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and is consistent with prior knowledge.

claim: Consecutive arrays of TPR motifs fold into a TPR superhelical structure with a pitch of seven TPR motifs.
source: Consecutive arrays of TPR motifs fold into a TPR superhelical structure with a pitch of seven TPR motifs (Das et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Each of the three TPR proteins of the TPR lobe homo-dimerise through their N-terminal TPR helix.
source: Each of the three TPR proteins of the TPR lobe homo-dimerise through their N-terminal TPR helix.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The two C-terminal TPR helices of the APC3 homo-dimer provide the IR-tail binding site for coactivators and APC10.
source: The two C-terminal TPR helices of the APC3 homo-dimer provide the IR-tail binding site for coactivators and APC10 (Chang et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015; Matyskiela and Morgan, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by prior structural studies cited in the manuscript and observed in the current structure.

claim: Structurally equivalent sites on APC8 interact with the C-box of coactivator N-terminal domains.
source: whereas structurally equivalent sites on APC8 interacts with the C-box of coactivator N-terminal domains (NTDs) (Chang et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by prior structural studies cited in the manuscript and observed in the current structure.

claim: Assembly of the complete APC/C complex is augmented by four small non-globular intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs).
source: Assembly of the complete APC/C complex is augmented by four small non-globular intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) that by interacting simultaneously with multiple large globular subunits stabilise the APC/C.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and supported by prior knowledge.

claim: Cryo-EM density bridging the CDH1 WD40 domain and APC10 corresponds to the D-box degron of Hsl1.
source: Cryo-EM density bridging the CDH1 WD40 domain (CDH1WD40) and APC10 corresponds to the D-box degron of Hsl1 (da Fonseca et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density and consistent with prior studies.

claim: In all three states, the APC2:APC11 catalytic module adopts an upward conformation that positions the APC11 RING domain proximal (~30 Å) to the substrate.
source: In all three states, the APC2:APC11 catalytic module adopts an upward conformation that positions the APC11 RING domain (APC11RING) proximal (~30 Å) to the substrate (Figures 1—3), similar to that observed in the active human APC/CCDH1:EMI1 complex (Figure 4A and B; Chang et al., 2015; Höfler et al., 2024).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: A recent analysis of human APC/CCDH1:EMI1 determined at 2.9 Å resolution revealed a zinc-binding module (APC2ZBM) inserted within cullin repeat 2 (CR2) of APC2.
source: A recent analysis of human APC/CCDH1:EMI1 determined at 2.9 Å resolution revealed a zinc-binding module (APC2ZBM) inserted within cullin repeat 2 (CR2) of APC2 (Höfler et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on a prior study cited in the manuscript.

claim: APC2ZBM constitutes a 45-residue insert between the A and B α-helices of CR2.
source: This segment constitutes a 45-residue insert between the A and B α-helices of CR2 (Figure 5A), and is most similar in structure to treble-clef/GATA-like zinc fingers.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of human APC2 from a prior study.

claim: Four Cys residues coordinate the zinc ion in human APC2ZBM.
source: Four Cys residues coordinate the zinc ion in human APC2.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of human APC2 from a prior study.

claim: APC2ZBM is conserved within metazoan APC2 sequences (from humans to C. elegans), but not in yeast APC2 sequences.
source: A multiple sequence alignment showed that APC2ZBM is conserved within metazoan APC2 sequences (from humans to C. elegans), but not in yeast APC2 sequences (Chang et al., 2015; Höfler et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis cited in the manuscript.

claim: There is no structural equivalent of human APC2ZBM in the cryo-EM structure of S. cerevisiae APC/CCDH1:Hsl1.
source: Consistent with this analysis, there is no structural equivalent of human APC2ZBM in the cryo-EM structure of S. cerevisiae APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the S. cerevisiae structure presented in the manuscript.

claim: APC2ZBM substantially increases the thermal stability of human APC2.
source: APC2ZBM substantially increases the thermal stability of human APC2.
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies of human APC2.

claim: The C-terminal domain (CTD) of APC2 (APC2CTD), together with the associated APC11 subunit, are less well defined than other regions of the complex.
source: Similarly to human APC/C structures, the C-terminal domain (CTD) of APC2 (APC2CTD), together with the associated APC11 subunit, are less well defined than other regions of the complex, with the WHB domain of APC2 (APC2WHB) being highly flexible and not visible in cryo-EM density (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: The WHB domain of APC2 (APC2WHB) is highly flexible and not visible in cryo-EM density.
source: Similarly to human APC/C structures, the C-terminal domain (CTD) of APC2 (APC2CTD), together with the associated APC11 subunit, are less well defined than other regions of the complex, with the WHB domain of APC2 (APC2WHB) being highly flexible and not visible in cryo-EM density (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: In human APC/C structures, APC2WHB is flexible when not in complex with the priming E2 (UbcH10) or bound to the MCC.
source: In human APC/C structures, APC2WHB is likewise flexible when not in complex with the priming E2 (UbcH10) or bound to the MCC (Brown et al., 2015; Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: APC2WHB becomes ordered when the APC/C forms complexes with either UbcH10, the MCC, Nek2A, or when SUMOylated.
source: APC2WHB becomes ordered when the APC/C forms complexes with either UbcH10 (Brown et al., 2015), the MCC (Alfieri et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2016), Nek2A (Alfieri et al., 2020), or SUMOylated (Yatskevich et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The APC4 subunit comprises a WD40 domain with a long four-helix bundle insert between blades 3 and 4.
source: The APC4 subunit comprises a WD40 domain with a long four-helix bundle insert between blades 3 and 4, augmented by an insert within blade 3 that is an α-helix in human APC4 and a β-hairpin in S. cerevisiae APC4 (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, the APC4 WD40 domain (APC4WD40) is constructed from six blades, in contrast to human APC4 which incorporates a typical seven-β-bladed propeller.
source: Strikingly, in contrast to human APC4 which incorporates a typical seven-β-bladed propeller, in S. cerevisiae the APC4 WD40 domain (APC4WD40) is constructed from six blades (blades 1–6; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the S. cerevisiae structure presented in the manuscript.

claim: The absence of cryo-EM density for a blade7 in S. cerevisiae APC4 is supported by an AlphaFold2 prediction.
source: The absence of cryo-EM density for a blade7 in S. cerevisiae APC4 is supported by an AlphaFold2 prediction (Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2021; Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by both cryo-EM data and computational prediction.

claim: The unusual APC4WD40 domain architecture might be specific to S. cerevisiae.
source: The unusual APC4WD40 domain architecture might be specific to S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is speculated based on comparison with other species.

claim: The AlphaFold2 prediction of S. pombe APC4 proposes a seven-bladed WD40 domain.
source: The AlphaFold2 prediction of S. pombe APC4 proposes a seven-bladed WD40 domain (Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction cited in the manuscript.

claim: APC1 is the largest APC/C subunit (1748 residues in S. cerevisiae).
source: APC1, the largest APC/C subunit (1748 residues in S. cerevisiae), is composed of an N-terminal WD40 β-propeller domain (APC1WD40) and a toroidal PC domain (proteosome/cyclosome; APC1PC) interconnected by a predominantly α-helical solenoid domain (APC1Mid).
evidence: This is directly stated and observed in the structure.

claim: APC1 is composed of an N-terminal WD40 β-propeller domain (APC1WD40) and a toroidal PC domain (APC1PC) interconnected by a predominantly α-helical solenoid domain (APC1Mid).
source: APC1, the largest APC/C subunit (1748 residues in S. cerevisiae), is composed of an N-terminal WD40 β-propeller domain (APC1WD40) and a toroidal PC domain (proteosome/cyclosome; APC1PC) interconnected by a predominantly α-helical solenoid domain (APC1Mid).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: APC5 comprises an N-terminal α-helical domain and C-terminal TPR domain of 13 TPR motifs generating two TPR helical turns.
source: APC5 comprises an N-terminal α-helical domain and C-terminal TPR domain of 13 TPR motifs generating two TPR helical turns.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: APC10 is a DOC homology domain comprising a β-sandwich homologous to galactose-binding domains.
source: APC10 is a DOC homology domain comprising a β-sandwich homologous to galactose-binding domains (Au et al., 2002; Wendt et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The four smaller non-globular subunits (APC9, CDC26/APC12, SWM1/APC13, MND2) have a high content of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
source: Our structure indicates how the four smaller non-globular subunits (APC9, CDC26/APC12, SWM1/APC13, MND2) (Hall et al., 2003; Passmore et al., 2003; Zachariae et al., 1998b; Zachariae et al., 1996), with a high content of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), mediate inter-subunit interactions between the larger globular subunits (Figure 4).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and consistent with prior knowledge.

claim: CDC26/APC12 and SWM1/APC13 share sequence conservation with their metazoan counterparts.
source: CDC26/APC12 and SWM1/APC13 share sequence conservation with their metazoan counterparts (Schwickart et al., 2004; Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis cited in the manuscript.

claim: SWM1 is the ortholog of metazoan APC13.
source: consistent with the proposal that SWM1 is the ortholog of metazoan APC13 (Hall et al., 2003; Passmore et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: MND2 is the S. cerevisiae ortholog of human APC15.
source: consistent with the proposal that MND2 is the S. cerevisiae ortholog of human APC15 (Mansfeld et al., 2011)
evidence: This is based on prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: MND2 and APC15 share related functions in promoting the auto-ubiquitylation of CDC20 in the context of the S. cerevisiae and human APC/C:MCC complexes.
source: and that MND2 and APC15 share related functions in promoting the auto-ubiquitylation of CDC20 in the context of the S. cerevisiae and human APC/C:MCC complexes (Alfieri et al., 2016; Foster and Morgan, 2012; Mansfeld et al., 2011; Uzunova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: APC9 is required for the efficient incorporation of CDC27/APC3 into the assembled APC/C.
source: Analysis of the subunit composition of APC/C complexes purified from S. cerevisiae strains harbouring specific gene deletions revealed that APC9 is required for the efficient incorporation of CDC27/APC3 into the assembled APC/C (Passmore et al., 2003; Zachariae et al., 1998b)
evidence: This is based on prior genetic studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: SWM1/APC13 and CDC26/APC12 are required for the stoichiometric assembly of APC3, APC6 and APC9 into the complex.
source: whereas SWM1/APC13 and CDC26/APC12 are required for the stoichiometric assembly of APC3, APC6 and APC9 into the complex (Schwickart et al., 2004; Zachariae et al., 1998b).
evidence: This is based on prior genetic studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The N-terminal 13 residues of CDC26/APC12 insert into the TPR groove of APC6, adopting an extended conformation.
source: The N-terminal 13 residues of CDC26/APC12 insert into the TPR groove of APC6, adopting an extended conformation and mode of binding highly conserved with previous cryo-EM and crystallographic structures of human and S. pombe orthologs (Chang et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010a; Figure 4)
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and consistent with prior studies.

claim: CDC26/APC12 folds into an α-helix that packs against α-helices of the inner groove of the APC6 TPR super-helix.
source: CDC26/APC12 then folds into an α-helix that packs against α-helices of the inner groove of the APC6 TPR super-helix, similar to the human and S. pombe APC6:APC12 complexes, as is the disordered C-terminus of CDC26/APC12.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and consistent with prior studies.

claim: The role of CDC26/APC12 in stabilising the association of APC3, APC6 and APC9 with the APC/C complex is likely through its specific role in stabilising the APC6 TPR super-helix.
source: Thus, the role of CDC26/APC12 in stabilising the association of APC3, APC6 and APC9 with the APC/C complex (Schwickart et al., 2004; Zachariae et al., 1998b) is likely through its specific role in stabilising the APC6 TPR super-helix (Wang et al., 2009) which bridges APC3 with APC8 (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and prior functional studies.

claim: In human APC/C, the APC13 N-terminus inserts into the TPR groove formed by the N-terminal TPR helix of APC8A.
source: In human APC/C, the APC13 N-terminus inserts into the TPR groove formed by the N-terminal TPR helix of APC8A (Brown et al., 2015; Chang et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The extended chain of APC13 interacts with structurally equivalent symmetry-related shallow grooves on the outer TPR-helical ridges of APC8B, APC6A, APC6B, and APC3A.
source: The extended chain of APC13 then interacts with structurally equivalent symmetry-related shallow grooves present on the outer TPR-helical ridges of APC8B, APC6A, APC6B, and APC3A (sites 4–7, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: These shallow grooves are lined with side chains of aromatic residues that engage hydrophobic residues of APC13.
source: These shallow grooves are lined with side chains of aromatic residues that engage hydrophobic residues of APC13 (Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: S. cerevisiae APC13 engages the structurally equivalent sites on APC8B, APC6A, APC6B, and APC3A (sites 4–7).
source: Similar to human APC13, S. cerevisiae APC13 engages the structurally equivalent sites on APC8B, APC6A, APC6B, and APC3A (sites 4–7, Figure 4E)
evidence: This is directly observed in the S. cerevisiae structure.

claim: The N-terminus of S. cerevisiae APC13 inserts into the TPR groove of APC8A.
source: with its N-terminus also inserting into the TPR groove of APC8A.
evidence: This is directly observed in the S. cerevisiae structure.

claim: Human APC13 and S. cerevisiae SWM1/APC13 perform comparable structural roles, contacting the successive TPR subunits of the TPR lobe.
source: Human APC13 and S. cerevisiae SWM1/APC13 perform comparable structural roles, contacting the successive TPR subunits of the TPR lobe.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: The conserved structural roles of APC13 explain the ability of human APC13 to substitute for the function of S. cerevisiae SWM1/APC13 in vivo.
source: Although human and S. cerevisiae APC13 share only low sequence similarity (Supplementary file 1b), their conserved structural roles presumably explains the ability of human APC13 to substitute for the function of S. cerevisiae SWM1/APC13 in vivo (Penkner et al., 2005; Schwickart et al., 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and prior functional studies.

claim: In human APC/C, APC16 is visible as a single 40-residue extended α-helix that lies along the shallow grooves on the outer TPR-helical ridges of APC3B, APC7A and APC7B.
source: In human APC/C, APC16 is visible as a single 40-residue extended α-helix that lies along the shallow grooves on the outer TPR-helical ridges of APC3B, APC7A and APC7B (sites 1-3, Figure 4F), forming equivalent interactions as observed for APC13 contacts with APC3, APC6 and APC8 (Brown et al., 2015; Chang et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: S. cerevisiae APC9 is over twice the size of APC16.
source: S. cerevisiae APC9 is over twice the size of APC16 with the two proteins sharing no clear sequence similarity.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: 131 of 265 residues of APC9 were built into the S. cerevisiae APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 cryo-EM map as three discontinuous segments.
source: Guided by an AlphaFold2 prediction of APC9 (Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2021) and a complex of APC9 and APC3 (Jumper et al., 2021), we built 131 of 265 residues into the S. cerevisiae APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 cryo-EM map as three discontinuous segments (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the structural data.

claim: The C-terminal segment (segment 3) of APC9 is a short three-turn α-helix that is structurally homologous to the mode of human APC16 binding to APC3B.
source: The C-terminal segment (segment 3) is a short three-turn α-helix that is structurally homologous to the mode of human APC16 binding to APC3B (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure through comparison.

claim: Segment 2 of APC9, composed of three separated α-helices, docks onto the outer surface of APC3A, bridging the two turns of the TPR helix.
source: Segment 2, composed of three separated α-helices, docks onto the outer surface of APC3A, bridging the two turns of the TPR helix (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: Segment 1 of APC9 bridges APC3A and APC6A.
source: Finally, segment 1 bridges APC3A and APC6A (Figure 4C insert), likely explaining why APC9 deletion causes loss of both APC3 and APC9 from purified APC/C complexes (Passmore et al., 2003; Zachariae et al., 1998b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and explains prior genetic observations.

claim: In human APC/C, the N-terminus of APC15 inserts as an extended chain into the groove formed by the N-terminal TPR helix of APC5.
source: In human APC/C, the visible regions of APC15 adopt a relatively simple elongated structure, with the N-terminus of the protein inserting as an extended chain into the groove formed by the N-terminal TPR helix of APC5, then forming an α-helix (APC15NTH) that contacts the N-terminal α-helical domain of APC5, before engaging a groove at the interface of APC6A and APC8A.
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies of human APC/C.

claim: S. cerevisiae MND2/APC15 contacts the N-terminal α-helical domain of APC5, and APC6A and APC8A, as for human APC15.
source: S. cerevisiae MND2/APC15 also contacts the N-terminal α-helical domain of APC5, and APC6A and APC8A, as for human APC15, but has an overall more irregular structure, with its N-terminus docking into a groove formed between the APC5 TPR helix and the four-helical bundle of APC4 (Figure 4A, C and E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the S. cerevisiae structure.

claim: An insert of S. cerevisiae APC15, not conserved in human, protrudes into the APC/C cavity, engaging the outer TPR helix of APC8B that forms the C-box binding site.
source: An insert of S. cerevisiae APC15, not conserved in human, protrudes into the APC/C cavity, engaging the outer TPR helix of APC8B that forms the C-box binding site (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the S. cerevisiae structure.

claim: A stretch of ~40 acidic residues, common to both human and S. cerevisiae APC15, is C-terminal to the ordered regions of APC15 in both complexes.
source: A stretch of ~40 acidic residues, common to both human and S. cerevisiae APC15, is C-terminal to the ordered regions of APC15 in both complexes.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural observations.

claim: In the human APC/CMCC structure, the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC) was observed to adopt both closed and open conformations.
source: In the human APC/CMCC structure, the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC) was observed to adopt both closed and open conformations (APC/CMCC-closed and APC/CMCC-open), with APC/CMCC-closed being associated with disorder of APC15NTH and concomitant conformational changes of APC4 and APC5, whereas an ordered APC15NTH is associated with APC/CMCC-open (Alfieri et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: APC15NTH is structurally conserved in S. cerevisiae APC/C.
source: Our observation that APC15NTH is structurally conserved in S. cerevisiae APC/C (Figure 4E) is consistent with a defect in CDC20MCC ubiquitylation caused by deleting APC15 (Foster and Morgan, 2012).
evidence: This is directly observed in the S. cerevisiae structure and consistent with prior functional studies.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, MND2 specifically suppresses securin/Pds1 ubiquitylation by the Ama1 coactivator-APC/C complex that prevents premature sister chromatid segregation during meiosis.
source: In contrast to MND2/APC15 promoting CDC20MCC ubiquitylation during the SAC, in S. cerevisiae, MND2 specifically suppresses securin/Pds1 ubiquitylation by the Ama1 coactivator-APC/C complex that prevents premature sister chromatid segregation during meiosis (Oelschlaegel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The 14 sites of MND2 phosphorylation required for efficient APC/CAma1-regulated progression through meiosis I are located within, and C-terminal to, the acidic stretch in MND2.
source: The 14 sites of MND2 phosphorylation required for efficient APC/CAma1-regulated progression through meiosis I (Torres and Borchers, 2007), are located within, and C-terminal to, the acidic stretch in MND2, and are therefore not visible in our structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the structure and prior functional studies.

claim: CDC26/APC12, SWM1/APC13 and human APC15 are anchored at their N-termini by inserting into the TPR grooves of APC6, APC8A, and APC5, respectively.
source: CDC26/APC12, SWM1/APC13 and human APC15 are anchored at their N-termini by inserting into the TPR grooves of APC6, APC8A, and APC5, respectively (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structures.

claim: These interactions serve to stabilise the TPR groove through formation of protein-protein interactions.
source: These interactions serve to stabilise the TPR groove through formation of protein-protein interactions (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and prior studies.

claim: In human APC/C, a 40-residue loop of APC1WD40 inserts into the TPR groove of APC8B.
source: In human APC/C, a 40-residue loop of APC1WD40 inserts into the TPR groove of APC8B, although this structural feature is not conserved in S. cerevisiae APC/C.
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies of human APC/C.

claim: Coactivators interact with the APC/C through an N-terminal C-box motif and a C-terminal IR tail.
source: Coactivators interact with the APC/C through an N-terminal C-box motif (Schwab et al., 2001) and a C-terminal IR tail (Passmore et al., 2003; Vodermaier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Both the C-box and IR tail motifs are highly evolutionarily conserved.
source: Both motifs are highly evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The C-box binding site within the TPR helix of APC8B is structurally conserved with the IR-tail binding site on APC3.
source: Interestingly, although the seven-residue C-box and two-residue IR tail lack obvious sequence similarity, the C-box binding site within the TPR helix of APC8B is structurally conserved with the IR-tail binding site on APC3, with an Arg residue, common to both, anchoring the motifs to their respective binding sites (Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The docking of the coactivator C-box motif to APC8B/CDC23 rationalises the temperature-sensitive cell cycle mutations of S. cerevisiae CDC23.
source: The docking of the coactivator C-box motif to this site on APC8B/CDC23 rationalises the temperature-sensitive cell cycle mutations of S. cerevisiae CDC23 (Sikorski et al., 1990), and prior mutagenesis data implicating Asn405 of APC8/CDC23 in CDH1 binding (Matyskiela and Morgan, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and prior genetic/mutagenesis studies.

claim: When in complex with the APC/C, CDH1NTD folds into five α-helices (labelled α2-α6).
source: When in complex with the APC/C, CDH1NTD folds into five α-helices (labelled α2-α6; Figure 6).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: Four α-helices of CDH1NTD mediate APC/C – CDH1 interactions, three of which (α2, α3 and α6) form anti-parallel interactions with APC1PC α-helices and are conserved with human CDH1.
source: Four of these α-helices mediate APC/C – CDH1 interactions, three of which; α2, α3 and α6, that form anti-parallel interactions with APC1PC α-helices, being conserved with human CDH1 (Figure 6B and E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and through comparison with human CDH1.

claim: Unique to S. cerevisiae CDH1 is a three-turn α-helix (α5) that docks onto the outer TPR ridge of APC6B.
source: Unique to S. cerevisiae CDH1 is a three-turn α-helix (α5) that docks onto the outer TPR ridge of APC6B, running antiparallel to exposed α-helices, and bridging APC8B (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the S. cerevisiae structure.

claim: CDK phosphorylation of CDH1NTD inhibits CDH1 binding to the APC/C.
source: CDK phosphorylation of CDH1NTD inhibits CDH1 binding to the APC/C, and substituting alanines for all eleven predicted CDK sites in S. cerevisiae CDH1 almost completely eliminated CDH1 phosphorylation in mitosis (Zachariae et al., 1998a).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Mimicking six CDK phosphosites with aspartates abolished binding of CDH1 to the APC/C in vivo.
source: Mimicking six CDK phosphosites with aspartates abolished binding of CDH1 to the APC/C in vivo, whereas a mutant with non-phosphorylatable sites bound APC/C more tightly than wild type CDH1 (Höckner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Two CDK sites (Ser227, Ser239) are conserved in human CDH1 and map on or close to the α6 helix that docks onto APC1PC.
source: Two CDK sites (Ser227, Ser239) are conserved in human CDH1 (Figure 6B; Chang et al., 2015), and map on or close to the α6 helix that docks onto APC1PC (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on structural mapping and prior studies.

claim: Phosphorylation of either Ser227 or Ser239 in human CDH1 contributed significantly to CDH1 inactivation.
source: Phosphorylation of either site in human CDH1 contributed significantly to CDH1 inactivation (Chang et al., 2015), likely by disrupting CDH1NTD-APC1PC interactions.
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Three reported non-consensus CDK-phosphosites within α5 (Ser216, Ser220, Ser225) would likely interfere with α5 interactions with APC6B and APC8B.
source: Additionally, three reported non-consensus CDK-phosphosites within α5 (Ser216, Ser220, Ser225) (Hall et al., 2004) would likely interfere with α5 interactions with APC6B and APC8B (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and prior phosphorylation data.

claim: The recent 2.9 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of APC/CCDH1:EMI1 revealed an N-terminal amphipathic α-helix of CDH1 (CDH1α1) interacting through non-polar interactions with a hydrophobic groove in the APC1WD40 domain.
source: The recent 2.9 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of APC/CCDH1:EMI1 revealed an N-terminal amphipathic α-helix of CDH1 (CDH1α1) interacting through non-polar interactions with a hydrophobic groove in the APC1WD40 domain (Höfler et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on a prior structural study cited in the manuscript.

claim: The N-terminal α-helix (CDH1α1) is conserved in metazoan coactivators, but not present in S. cerevisiae CDH1.
source: This α-helix is conserved in metazoan coactivators, but consistent with MSA analysis, is not present in S. cerevisiae CDH1.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural observations.

claim: The mode of binding of CDH1IR to the IR-tail binding site on APC3A is conserved with that of human APC/CCDH1:EMI1.
source: Finally, the mode of binding of CDH1IR to the IR-tail binding site on APC3A is conserved with that of human APC/CCDH1:EMI1 (Brown et al., 2015; Chang et al., 2015; Höfler et al., 2024; Matyskiela and Morgan, 2009; Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is directly observed through structural comparison.

claim: APC9 segment 2 interactions with the C-terminal TPR helix of APC3A may stabilise the CDH1IR tail-binding site of APC3A.
source: APC9 segment 2 interactions with the C-terminal TPR helix of APC3A may stabilise the CDH1IR tail-binding site of APC3A.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: Coactivators function as substrate adaptors for both metazoan and S. cerevisiae APC/C.
source: Biochemical studies on both metazoan and S. cerevisiae APC/C revealed that coactivators function as substrate adaptors (Burton and Solomon, 2001; Hilioti et al., 2001; Kraft et al., 2005; Schwab et al., 2001), and also enhance APC/C catalytic activity (Kimata et al., 2008; Van Voorhis and Morgan, 2014).
evidence: This is based on prior biochemical studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: For S. cerevisiae APC/C, catalytic enhancement results from a substantially more efficient interaction of the APC/C with its E2s Ubc4 and Ubc1.
source: For S. cerevisiae APC/C, catalytic enhancement results from a substantially more efficient interaction of the APC/C with its E2s Ubc4 and Ubc1 (Van Voorhis and Morgan, 2014).
evidence: This is based on prior biochemical studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The affinity of the human APC/C for UbcH10 is increased three-fold when in complex with CDH1.
source: Similarly, the affinity of the human APC/C for UbcH10 is increased three-fold when in complex with CDH1 (Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on prior biochemical studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: In both unphosphorylated S. cerevisiae apo-APC/C and APC/CCDH1:Hsl1, the APC2:APC11 catalytic module adopts the same raised position.
source: Comparing unphosphorylated S. cerevisiae apo-APC/C and APC/CCDH1:Hsl1 cryo-EM structures showed that in both states the APC2:APC11 catalytic module adopts the same raised position (Figure 8A and B), similar to human APC/CCDH1:EMI1.
evidence: This is directly observed through structural comparison.

claim: The conformation of the APC2:APC11 catalytic module in apo-APC/C does not sterically occlude Ubc4 binding.
source: Docking Ubc4 onto the RING domain of APC11 (based on the S. cerevisiae Not4:Ubc4 coordinates; PDB 5AIE Bhaskar et al., 2015) indicated that the conformation of the APC2:APC11 catalytic module in apo-APC/C does not sterically occlude Ubc4 binding (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is based on molecular modeling using the structure.

claim: The mechanism by which coactivator stimulates S. cerevisiae APC/C catalytic activity through enhancing E2 binding differs from human APC/C.
source: Thus, the mechanism by which coactivator stimulates S. cerevisiae APC/C catalytic activity through enhancing E2 binding differs from human APC/C, although the structural mechanism is not defined in our study.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the human ternary complex, CDH1NTD disrupts the interaction between APC1PC and APC8B by binding to a site on APC1PC that overlaps the site in contact with APC8B.
source: In the human ternary complex, CDH1NTD disrupts the interaction between APC1PC and APC8B by binding to a site on APC1PC that overlaps the site in contact with APC8B.
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies of human APC/C.

claim: In S. cerevisiae apo-APC/C, the TPR lobe does not directly contact APC1PC.
source: In contrast to human APC/C, in the more open structure of S. cerevisiae apo-APC/C, the TPR lobe does not directly contact APC1PC, and thus the position of APC8B relative to the APC8B – CDH1NTD1-binding site does not impede CDH1 association.
evidence: This is directly observed in the S. cerevisiae structure.

claim: On binding to S. cerevisiae APC/C, CDH1NTD interconnects the TPR lobe with APC1PC to reinforce TPR and platform lobe interactions.
source: Instead, on binding to S. cerevisiae APC/C, of CDH1NTD interconnects the TPR lobe with APC1PC to reinforce TPR and platform lobe interactions (Figure 8A and B; lower panels).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: To accommodate closure of the APC/C cavity, conformational changes are distributed over the subunits of the TPR and platform lobes, including a tilt of APC1PC relative to the combined domains of APC1Mid-APC1WD40.
source: To accommodate closure of the APC/C cavity, conformational changes are distributed over the subunits of the TPR and platform lobes, including a tilt of APC1PC relative to the combined domains of APC1Mid-APC1WD40 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed through structural comparison.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of APC/C subunits APC1 and APC3 is required for CDC20 to activate the APC/C.
source: Hyperphosphorylation of APC/C subunits APC1 and APC3 is required for CDC20 to activate the APC/C (Fujimitsu et al., 2016; Golan et al., 2002; Kraft et al., 2005; Kramer et al., 2000; Lahav-Baratz et al., 1995; Qiao et al., 2016; Rudner and Murray, 2000; Shteinberg et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: In metazoan unphosphorylated apo-APC/C, an auto-inhibitory (AI) segment incorporated into the 300s loop of APC1 sterically occludes the C-box binding site on APC8B.
source: In metazoan unphosphorylated apo-APC/C, an auto-inhibitory (AI) segment incorporated into the 300s loop inserted within the WD40 domain of APC1 (APC1300L) sterically occludes the C-box binding site on APC8B (APC8C-box) thereby competing for CDC20 binding (Fujimitsu et al., 2016; Qiao et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation of residues within APC1300L, including the AI segment, displaces the AI segment from APC8C-box allowing CDC20 binding.
source: Phosphorylation of residues within (APC1300L), including the AI segment, displaces the AI segment from APC8C-box allowing CDC20 binding.
evidence: This is based on prior structural and functional studies.

claim: Deleting APC1300L constitutively activates APC/CCDC20.
source: Multiple lines of data support this model, including the observation of cryo-EM density for the AI segment bound to APC8C-box (Höfler et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2016b), the constitutive activation of APC/CCDC20 on deleting APC1300L, and the location of multiple CDK and PLK1 sites within APC1300L (Fujimitsu et al., 2016; Höfler et al., 2024; Li et al., 2016; Qiao et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Replacing phosphosites in APC1300L with glutamates activated APC/CCDC20.
source: Replacing these phosphosites with glutamates activated APC/CCDC20, whereas in contrast, mutations to Ala prevented CDK activation of APC/CCDC20 (Fujimitsu et al., 2016; Höfler et al., 2024; Qiao et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Deleting the APC1 WD40 loop of S. cerevisiae (residues 225-365), equivalent to human APC1300L, caused only a minor growth defect with no evidence for APC/C hyperactivation.
source: However, the Morgan lab recently reported that deleting the APC1 WD40 loop of S. cerevisiae (residues 225-365), equivalent to human APC1300L, caused only a minor growth defect, but importantly no evidence for APC/C hyperactivation (Ng et al., 2024)
evidence: This is based on a recent functional study cited in the manuscript.

claim: Superimposing both apo-APC/C states (phosphorylated and unphosphorylated) reveals that the only obvious difference between the two is a small relative shift of the TPR lobe.
source: Superimposing both apo-APC/C states (phosphorylated and unphosphorylated) reveals that the only obvious difference between the two is a small relative shift of the TPR lobe (Figure 9C–E).
evidence: This is directly observed through structural comparison.

claim: Phosphorylated regions of S. cerevisiae APC/C might contact CDC20 directly or indirectly to enhance its binding.
source: It is possible that in contrast to the activation of human APC/CCDC20 through release of a negative auto-inhibitory segment, phosphorylated regions of S. cerevisiae APC/C might contact CDC20 directly or indirectly to enhance its binding.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural observations.

claim: The largest difference between human and S. cerevisiae APC/C is the absence of an APC7 homolog in S. cerevisiae.
source: We present a comparative study of human and S. cerevisiae APC/C. This revealed a similar overall architecture, with the largest difference being the absence of an APC7 homolog in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is directly stated based on the structural comparison.

claim: A recent study discovered a specific role for APC7 in mammalian brain development.
source: A recent study discovered a specific role for APC7 in mammalian brain development (Ferguson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on a prior study cited in the manuscript.

claim: Homozygous ANAPC7 mutations in humans, leading to loss of APC7 protein, underlies an inherited intellectual disability syndrome.
source: Homozygous ANAPC7 mutations in humans, leading to loss of APC7 protein, underlies an inherited intellectual disability syndrome, caused by defective APC/CΔAPC7-mediated degradation of the chromosome-associated protein Ki-67 (Ferguson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on a prior study cited in the manuscript.

claim: In mammals, APC7 confers specific post-mitotic functions in the developing brain through selective protein-recognition.
source: Thus in mammals, APC7 confers specific post-mitotic functions in the developing brain through selective protein-recognition.
evidence: This is inferred from the prior study on APC7 function.

claim: The mode of binding of the CDH1 coactivator subunit is very similar between human and S. cerevisiae APC/C, except for the presence in human APC/C of the N-terminal α-helix (CDH1α1).
source: The mode of binding of the CDH1 coactivator subunit is also very similar, except for the presence in human APC/C of the N-terminal α-helix (CDH1α1), not conserved in S. cerevisiae APC/C, that mediates contacts to APC1WD40.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mechanism of inactivation of CDH1 by CDK phosphorylation of two conserved serine residues on CDH1 at the CDH1NTD – APC1PC interface is conserved.
source: Also conserved is the mechanism of inactivation of CDH1 by CDK phosphorylation of two conserved serine residues on CDH1 at the CDH1NTD – APC1PC interface.
evidence: This is based on structural and functional comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mechanism of stimulating CDC20-binding to the APC/C through phosphorylation-dependent relief of an auto-inhibitory segment of APC1 is not conserved in S. cerevisiae APC/C.
source: Finally, the mechanism of stimulating CDC20-binding to the APC/C through phosphorylation-dependent relief of an auto-inhibitory segment of APC1, as in human APC/C (Fujimitsu et al., 2016; Qiao et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016b), is not conserved in S. cerevisiae APC/C, a structural finding that is consistent with in vivo data (Ng et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on structural observations and prior functional studies.
